After months of speculation that she would leave before her eight-year term ends in October 2027, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde announced today that she will step down on February 7, 2027, just hours ahead of the Governing Council’s latest rate decision, according to Bloomberg. Hers is the third of the six Executive Board seats set to turn over by May.

Lagarde becomes only the second president in the ECB’s 28-year history to leave early, after Wim Duisenberg, whose shortened stint had been agreed in advance to break a France-Germany deadlock before the bank’s launch.

Lagarde, 70, told fellow policymakers she wanted “greater freedom to express her views” because she could not stay neutral on developments in France ahead of its April presidential election, the Financial Times reported. She has ruled out running herself and has been in talks to chair the World Economic Forum. In a video message, she said she leaves with “a sense of good work done, and an ECB that is fit for the future,” per Bloomberg.

Three of the six Executive Board seats — the presidency, the chief economist and the markets portfolio — turn over by May. Isabel Schnabel is leaving a year early to join the International Monetary Fund and Philip Lane’s term expires in May, so governments will likely try to settle all three in one deal, with EU summits in November and December, per Bloomberg.

For the presidency, Spain is backing Pablo Hernández de Cos, general manager of the Bank for International Settlements and former Bank of Spain governor, while the Dutch government is backing former Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot, the FT reported. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg in October see De Cos as the favorite. Knot built a reputation as a hawk during the eurozone debt crisis but has since softened into a pragmatist seen as responsive to bond-market stress, according to The Wall Street Journal, which also noted that an outsider can’t be ruled out given Lagarde herself was a last-minute pick in a 2019 package deal.

The timing also lets President Emmanuel Macron help pick Lagarde’s successor before his final term ends, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen leading French polls, which risks accusations of political encroachment on the ECB’s independence, Bloomberg added. Banque de France’s governor also left early, with Macron naming his chief of staff, Emmanuel Moulin, to the post.

The news barely moved markets following the announcement. The euro was down 0.1% against the dollar at $1.114, per the FT, while the 10-year German Bund yield was 1 basis point lower at 3.36% and the French-German 10-year spread held at 154 basis points, according to Bloomberg. ▪ Off 0.75 pt or more in the other 4, two of them (Q4 ‘25 & Q1 ‘26) mostly from the federal shutdown
▪ Since 2014 (ex-2020), its average miss is 0.59 pt: within half a point half the time, within a point 84% of the time

▪ When GDPNow falls more than half a point in the final month (it’s down 1.75 pts from 5.02% on Sept 25), the actual print has come in above its final reading in 16 of 22 quarters
▪ In third quarters specifically, the print has come in above GDPNow’s final reading in 10 of 14 quarters (ex-2020), by an average of 0.31 pt

This quarter it has company: as of Friday, six of the seven major GDP trackers I follow were between 3.1% and 3.7%, with the NY Fed the outlier at 2.67%. All seven are well above the Blue Chip consensus of ~2.5%.

Bloomberg: America’s closest allies have nearly stopped buying Treasuries.

According to Bloomberg's analysis, countries that vote most often with the U.S. at the U.N. bought a net $174.3B of Treasury notes and bonds in January through August. That’s the least for the period since 2021, and down more than 60% from a year earlier.

▪️ Japan, the biggest foreign holder, bought just $389M, down 99%
▪️ South Korea sold $23.8B, its biggest January–August sale in records going back to 1977
▪️ Taiwan also sold more than it bought
▪️ Countries that vote least often with the U.S. bought $17.1B, ending four straight years of selling. China is still the biggest seller.

Hedge funds, banks and other private investors have filled the gap and now hold about 70% of federal debt. But they’re more sensitive to price.

State Street’s Masahiko Loo: the market “isn’t losing foreign buyers — it’s losing automatic buyers.”

This week’s auctions showed some other evidence. Indirect bidders, often used as a stand-in for foreign demand, took 45.7% of Monday’s 2-year (vs. a 58.3% average) and 60.1% of Tuesday’s 5-year (vs. 64%). The 7-year sells Thursday.

▪️ Cloud: $30.7 billion (+103% year over year) vs. $29.15 billion estimate; operating income $11.1 billion vs. $9.75 billion, a 36.2% margin

▪️ Free cash flow: −$9.1 billion vs. −$2.7 billion estimate; zero buybacks
